claims.claim: Polycrates was the bishop of Ephesus in the second century.
He lived approximately between AD 130 and AD 196.
He came from a family in which seven of his relatives had been bishops, making him the eighth bishop of that line.
Around AD 196 he presided over a synod of Asian bishops that met to discuss the proper date of the Paschal feast.
The work is a letter addressed to Victor, the bishop of Rome, defending the Quartodeciman practice of celebrating Pascha on the 14th of Nisan.
The letter was composed between AD 186 and AD 195.
Victor had proposed enforcing a uniform Sunday celebration of Easter and threatened to excommunicate the Asian churches that kept the 14th‑of‑Nisan practice.
The controversy recorded in the letter is known as the Quartodeciman controversy, pitting the Roman Sunday tradition against the Asian practice of celebrating on the Jewish Passover date.
In the letter Polycrates states that he had served the Lord for sixty‑five years at the time of writing.
He argues that the Asian churches have continuously observed the exact day of the Passover “neither adding nor taking away,” citing the apostolic tradition of Philip, John, Polycarp, and others.
